title: Seasonal influenza (WHO, IDSA and CDC)
subject: infectious-disease
summary: Treat severe or hospitalised influenza with oseltamivir as early as possible whatever the illness duration. For non-severe illness, WHO 2024 suggests single-dose baloxavir only for high-risk patients and no antiviral for others, whereas CDC and IDSA recommend oseltamivir for all higher-risk outpatients.

sections.title: Recognise and stratify risk
items: Non-severe influenza: sudden cough, fever, headache, myalgia, sore throat and malaise without features of severe disease; most people recover within a week.

Severe influenza (WHO): sepsis, septic shock, severe pneumonia, ARDS, multi-organ failure or exacerbation of a chronic illness, usually needing admission, oxygen, ventilation or vasopressors. Treat novel or zoonotic influenza A (for example H5N1) as severe.
WHO high risk of hospitalisation: age 65 or more, immunocompromise, cardiovascular, neurological or chronic respiratory disease. Extremely high risk: age 85 or more, or several major risk factors.
CDC/IDSA higher-risk groups also include pregnancy and up to 2 weeks postpartum, BMI 40 or more, diabetes and other metabolic, renal, hepatic or haematological disease, and long-term care residents.
Admit for hypoxaemia, respiratory distress, hypotension, confusion, inability to maintain hydration, or decompensation of a chronic disease.

sections.title: Testing
items: Suspected severe influenza: nucleic acid amplification test (RT-PCR) on a nasopharyngeal swab (WHO). In ventilated patients also test lower respiratory tract samples, as upper-airway tests can be negative (IDSA).
Non-severe illness: test (digital immunoassay or NAAT) only when the result will change management, for example in a high-risk patient; conventional rapid antigen tests miss many cases.
Never delay antiviral treatment in severe or high-risk patients while waiting for a result.
Admitted patients: blood count, renal and liver function, blood gas, chest X-ray; blood and sputum cultures when bacterial co-infection is possible.

sections.title: Severe or hospitalised influenza
items: Give oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days as soon as possible to every hospitalised or severely ill patient, regardless of symptom duration (WHO, CDC, IDSA). It can be given by nasogastric tube but not with ileus, gastric stasis, malabsorption or GI bleeding.
Consider a longer course for critical illness or immunocompromise, guided by clinical course and repeat testing.

WHO recommends against peramivir and zanamivir for severe influenza; IV peramivir is reserved for patients who cannot take or absorb oseltamivir. WHO suggests baloxavir only when oseltamivir is unavailable.

Do not give corticosteroids for influenza or influenza pneumonia (WHO, IDSA) unless another indication exists (such as refractory septic shock or an asthma or COPD exacerbation). WHO also advises against macrolides without bacterial infection, convalescent plasma and mTOR inhibitors.

Look for and treat bacterial co-infection (S. pneumoniae, S. aureus including MRSA, S. pyogenes) when pneumonia is severe at presentation, the patient worsens after initial improvement, or there is no improvement after 3 to 5 days of antiviral treatment (IDSA).
Supportive care: oxygen to target saturation, cautious fluids, and lung-protective ventilation for ARDS.

sections.title: Non-severe influenza (outpatients)
items: WHO 2024: high-risk patients, suggest baloxavir as a single oral dose within 2 days of onset; low-risk patients, no antiviral. WHO makes a strong recommendation against oseltamivir for non-severe influenza, having found no important effect on hospitalisation or death.

CDC and IDSA disagree: treat every higher-risk outpatient, including pregnant women, with an antiviral as early as possible (oseltamivir, inhaled zanamivir, IV peramivir or oral baloxavir); treatment may be considered for healthy outpatients seen within 48 hours.

Baloxavir: not recommended in pregnancy or breastfeeding; use with caution in immunocompromised patients because resistance can emerge. Do not co-administer with dairy products, antacids or supplements containing calcium, iron, magnesium or zinc.
No antibiotics for non-severe influenza with a low probability of bacterial infection (WHO strong recommendation). Symptomatic care with paracetamol and fluids.
Advise return for breathlessness, chest pain, confusion, fever persisting beyond 3 to 5 days, or improvement followed by worsening.

sections.title: Post-exposure prophylaxis and vaccination
items: WHO: offer prophylaxis only to asymptomatic people at extremely high risk (age 85 or more, or several risk factors) exposed within the previous 48 hours: baloxavir single dose or oseltamivir 75 mg once daily for 10 days.
CDC: oseltamivir 75 mg once daily for 7 days after the last known exposure; in institutional outbreaks (for example care homes) for at least 2 weeks and until 1 week after the last case.
Annual influenza vaccination for all high-risk adults, pregnant women and health workers, and for household contacts of high-risk people.
Infection control: droplet precautions, masks, hand hygiene and cohorting of inpatients with influenza.

sections.title: Renal dosing and special groups
items: Oseltamivir treatment by creatinine clearance (WHO): above 60 mL/min 75 mg twice daily; above 30 to 60, 30 mg twice daily; above 10 to 30, 30 mg once daily; 10 or less without dialysis, not recommended; haemodialysis 30 mg after each session; peritoneal dialysis a single 30 mg dose.

Oseltamivir prophylaxis by creatinine clearance (WHO): above 30 to 60 mL/min 30 mg once daily; above 10 to 30, 30 mg every second day; haemodialysis 30 mg after every second session; peritoneal dialysis 30 mg once weekly.
Pregnancy: oseltamivir is safe (more than 1000 first-trimester exposures without excess malformation); CDC treats promptly without waiting for tests. Baloxavir is not recommended.
Immunocompromised patients shed virus longer: treat longer, retest, and consider antiviral resistance if not improving.
India: MoHFW categorisation (A, B, C) uses oseltamivir for categories B and C and has not adopted the WHO 2024 baloxavir approach for outpatients; follow national guidance where it applies.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Withholding oseltamivir from hospitalised or severely ill patients because more than 48 hours have passed.
Waiting for PCR results before treating severe, pregnant or other high-risk patients.
Giving corticosteroids for influenza pneumonia, or missing secondary S. aureus or pneumococcal pneumonia.
Using baloxavir in pregnancy, or zanamivir in patients with asthma or COPD (bronchospasm).

drugs.name: Oseltamivir (treatment)
drugs.dose: 75 mg orally twice daily for 5 days (longer in severe illness or immunocompromise)
drugs.notes: Creatinine clearance above 30 to 60 mL/min 30 mg twice daily; above 10 to 30, 30 mg once daily; haemodialysis 30 mg after each session. Nausea common; take with food.

drugs.name: Oseltamivir (post-exposure prophylaxis)
drugs.dose: 75 mg orally once daily for 10 days (WHO) or for 7 days after the last exposure (CDC)
drugs.notes: Start within 48 hours of exposure. Reduce in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Baloxavir marboxil
drugs.dose: Single oral dose: 40 mg if 20 to 79 kg; 80 mg if 80 kg or more
drugs.notes: Within 2 days of onset (treatment) or exposure (prophylaxis). Not in pregnancy or breastfeeding; caution in immunocompromise.

drugs.name: Zanamivir (inhaled)
drugs.dose: 10 mg (two 5 mg inhalations) twice daily for 5 days
drugs.notes: Avoid in asthma or COPD. WHO recommends against it for severe influenza.

drugs.name: Peramivir
drugs.dose: 600 mg IV as a single dose; creatinine clearance 30 to 49 mL/min 200 mg; 10 to 29 mL/min 100 mg
drugs.notes: Only when oral oseltamivir cannot be taken or absorbed (WHO).

drugs.name: Paracetamol
drugs.dose: 500 mg to 1 g orally every 4 to 6 hours as needed, maximum 4 g/day
drugs.notes: Lower maximum in liver disease, low body weight or alcohol dependence.
